Commuting statistics are not your route: budget attendance, fares and travel hours separately

Read Canadian main-mode shares beside group mean commute times, then build a separate hypothetical comparison of a monthly pass, pay-per-use transit and avoidable car cash.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Build an independent attendance, fare and travel-time scenario

Interactive planning lab

Pass cash across included months$1,920
Pay-per-use transit cash$1,152
Avoidable car commuting cash$2,592
Travel hours for the independently entered route192.0

The first two charts retain a fixed May 2025 Statistics Canada snapshot, released 26 August 2025 and reviewed 25 October 2026. The selected main-mode shares and group means do not change with the personal controls. Commuters usually work most hours outside the home; the survey population is ages 15–69 in the provinces, with the source exclusions stated below. The selected shares are not a complete partition and are not renormalized. No confidence intervals or causal estimates are calculated. The last two charts are original hypothetical calculations using independent inputs, not source fare or route estimates. Every included month has the same number of on-site days. A pass is bought in every included month, including one with zero on-site days, and covers every modeled transit trip. Per-use fare is the complete return-trip cash, without fare caps, transfers, concessions or non-work travel. Car cash includes only costs actually avoided when a return commute is not made; purchase cost, financing, retained insurance and other continuing ownership costs are excluded. One independently entered route takes the same time in both directions, including all travel components the reader supplies. Time is not converted into wages or available bank cash. The alternatives are separate scenarios and are not added together. No tax deduction, employer reimbursement, future fare inflation or recommendation of a travel mode is calculated.

The central idea

A group’s average trip cannot price your route. Attendance changes some commuting costs; a committed pass and continuing car ownership costs need their own treatment.

01

Start with the people represented by the statistic

A commuting headline can prompt a useful budget review, but its population is not a household travel diary. The statistical panels retain a Statistics Canada May 2025 snapshot, released on 26 August 2025.

Here, commuters are employed people usually working most hours outside the home. The supplement covers ages 15–69 in the provinces, excluding people on reserves, full-time Canadian Armed Forces members and people in institutions.

The first chart selects three main-mode shares: car, truck or van at 80.9%, public transit at 11.9%, and walking or cycling at 6.2%. Other methods are omitted. These figures are not percentages of all adults or a reader’s chances of travelling by a particular method.

Keep the reference month visible. A review date in 2026 does not turn May 2025 observations into a current personal schedule. The controls below leave the six published values unchanged.

02

Read the duration bars as group means, rather than a route experiment

The second panel gives mean trip-to-work times of 24.7 minutes for car commuters, 44.1 for public transit and 15.0 for active transport. The May 2025 questionnaire asks about the trip to work, rather than the complete return journey.

These are different groups, rather than the same travellers randomly assigned to transport methods. They do not establish how much time one person would save by changing modes. No confidence intervals or causal effects are calculated here.

For a personal comparison, measure the actual alternatives from the same starting point to the same destination. Include walking to a stop, waiting, transfers, finding parking and getting from the vehicle to the workplace. A quoted station-to-station journey may omit substantial parts of the trip.

Also record whether the return journey differs. The calculator uses one entered time for each direction to keep the arithmetic inspectable. If the outward trip takes thirty minutes and the return takes fifty, an average of forty per direction reproduces eighty daily minutes, but it does not describe either trip’s reliability.

03

Specify the attendance calendar before multiplying a daily cost

The default scenario assumes twelve on-site days in each of twelve identical months. That gives 144 complete return commutes. It is an original planning assumption, rather than an attendance estimate from the survey.

The number of included months matters. A seasonal job, a course or a temporary assignment may require only part of a year. Change that control to describe the intended window, then consider whether each included month really has the same attendance.

Holidays, vacation, illness, work travel and changes in a hybrid agreement can alter the actual count. For implementation, replace a repeated monthly assumption with the known calendar. Do not automatically multiply five days by fifty-two weeks if the person does not make that many trips.

The model compares three separate ways of paying for the stated commuting need. It does not combine their costs as though the same person simultaneously made all three complete journeys. Nor does it assume that each alternative is available or suitable for the actual route.

04

Compare the pass with the complete return fare at the same attendance

The invented monthly pass costs CAD 160 and is purchased in every included month. Across twelve months, its cash cost is CAD 1,920. The assumed complete return fare is CAD 8, so 144 pay-per-use commutes cost CAD 1,152.

At these inputs, the per-use scenario requires CAD 768 less cash over the window. That difference follows from the stated prices and attendance. It is not a statement about a real transit system or the best choice for every traveller.

The monthly crossing is CAD 160 ÷ CAD 8 = twenty complete return commutes. At twenty on-site days, both alternatives cost CAD 160 per month. Below that count the per-use line is lower; above it the pass line is lower within the stated model.

The pass line remains positive at zero on-site days because the scenario still buys it. If the pass can be skipped, cancelled or refunded for an unused month, use a different purchase calendar. A line describing an already committed payment cannot silently assume that refund.

05

Check the terms that a simple crossing leaves out

Actual fares may depend on zones, concessions, transfers, payment method, daily caps or monthly caps. A return journey might not cost twice a single fare, and automatic capping can change the shape of a per-use line.

The entered fare should represent the cash actually charged for one complete commuting day under the assumed terms. This calculator has no tariff engine. A zero per-use fare is permitted, but then dividing the pass price by that fare does not produce a finite crossing.

A pass may also cover useful non-work journeys. Those trips are excluded here so the attendance comparison remains specific. If the decision includes evenings and weekends, add that actual travel need and its alternative cash cost before deciding what the pass would replace.

Employer reimbursements, payroll deductions and tax effects also need separate evidence. The displayed amounts are assumed cash prices without those adjustments. A workplace benefit cannot be inferred from the national transport statistics.

06

Separate the cash avoided on a commuting day from continuing ownership costs

The invented car input is CAD 18 of avoidable cash for each complete return commute. At 144 commuting days, the displayed amount is CAD 2,592. This might represent genuinely avoidable fuel, parking or toll payments in a separately documented scenario.

A prepaid parking contract does not become a daily saving merely because the car stays home. Similarly, financing payments or retained insurance can continue while a person takes transit. Include a cost in the avoidable daily input only when the assumed change actually removes that cash payment.

The car line excludes those continuing costs. It therefore cannot answer whether to buy, sell or retain a vehicle, or rank the total economic cost of car ownership against transit. Depreciation, maintenance, insurance and disposal would require their own model and evidence.

This distinction prevents a common budget error: describing every allocated ownership expense as immediately spendable cash saved by one fewer drive. Allocation is useful for understanding costs, but the bank balance changes only when an actual payment changes.

07

Keep travel hours visible without booking them as income

The independent time input defaults to forty minutes in each direction. With 144 commuting days, that is 2 × 40 × 144 ÷ 60 = 192 travel hours across the included months.

The matrix varies attendance and one-way duration while retaining the number of included months. It shows why a modest daily difference can accumulate, and why the number of journeys matters alongside the duration of each journey.

Hours saved can matter for care, rest, study or other commitments. They do not automatically become paid work or an amount available to cover a bill. This article therefore keeps hours in their own unit and does not multiply them by a salary.

Before changing a travel plan, check the actual route, schedule, access needs, fare terms and payments that can be avoided. Use the published charts as context and the independently entered calendar as an explicit scenario. Revisit both when work arrangements or transport terms change.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Two charts retain six published May 2025 Canadian commuting figures. Two original scenario charts vary attendance cash and travel hours. Personal inputs do not alter the statistics or reproduce a real transit tariff. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Number of Canadian commuters increases for fourth straight year in 2025 ↗

    Released 26 August 2025; public HTML reviewed and retained 25 October 2026. Six selected figures describe main-mode shares and mean trip-to-work times for May 2025. The supplement universe and commuter definition are retained. The selected shares omit other methods; no intervals, trend significance or causal mode-switch effect is calculated.

  2. Statistics Canada · Labour Market Indicators — May 2025 questionnaire ↗

    Modified 8 May 2025; reviewed 25 October 2026. WFH_Q03 identifies the location with most usual hours, CCOMM_Q02 asks for the main commuting mode, and CCOMM_Q04 asks for minutes on the trip to work. This questionnaire supplies definitions rather than fare or route estimates. All cash prices, attendance and personal times in the scenario are invented.
